## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.101173.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.101173.3.sa1)

Summary:

In this work Ritchie and colleagues explore functional consequences of neuronal over-expression or deletion of the MAP3K DLK that their labs and others have strongly implicated in both axon degeneration, neuronal cell death, and axon regeneration. Their recent work in eLife (Li, 2021) showed that inducible over-expression of DLK (or the related LZK) induces neuronal death in the cerebellum. Here, they extend this work to show that inducible over-expression in Vglut1+ neuron also kills excitatory neurons in hippocampal CA1, but not CA3. They complement this very interesting finding with translatomics to quantify genes whose mRNAs are differentially translated in the context of DLK over-expression or knockout, the latter manipulation having little to no effect on the phenotypes measured. The authors note that several genes and pathways are differentially regulated according to whether DLK is over-expressed or knocked out. They note DLK-dependent changes in genes related to synaptic function and to the cytoskeleton and ultimately relate this in cultured neurons to findings that DLK over-expression negatively impacts synapse number and changes microtubules and neurites, though with a less obvious correlation.

Strengths:

Where this work represents a conceptual advance is in defining DLK-dependent changes in translation. Moreover, the finding that DLK may differentially impact neuronal death will become the basis for future studies exploring whether DLK contributes to differential neuronal susceptibility to death, which is a broadly important topic.

Comments on the latest version:

The addition of the P10 data is an important advance. With this, the authors have satisfactorily addressed the concerns that I raised.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.101173.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.101173.3.sa2)

This manuscript describes the impact of deleting or enhancing the expression of the neuronal-specific kinase DLK in glutamatergic hippocampal neurons using clever genetic strategies, which demonstrates that DLK deletion had minimal effects while overexpression resulted in neurodegeneration in vivo. To determine the molecular mechanisms underlying this effect, ribotag mice were used to determine changes in active translation which identified Jun and STMN4 as DLK-dependent genes that may contribute to this effect. Finally, experiments in cultured neurons were conducted to better understand the in vivo effects. These experiments demonstrated that DLK overexpression resulted in morphological and synaptic abnormalities.

Strengths:

This study provides interesting new insights into the role of DLK in the normal function of hippocampal neurons. Specifically, the study identifies:

(1) CA1 vs CA3 hippocampal neurons have differing sensitivity to increased DLK signaling.

(2) DLK-dependent signaling in these neurons is similar to but distinct from the downstream factors identified in other cell types, highlighted by the identification of STMN4 as a downstream signal.

(3) DLK overexpression in hippocampal neurons results in signaling that is similar to that induced by neuronal injury.

The study also provides confirmatory evidence that supports previously published work through orthogonal methods, which adds additional confidence to our understanding of DLK signaling in neurons. Taken together, this is a useful addition to our understanding of DLK function.

Comments on the latest version:

The authors have sufficiently addressed all issues raised with the initial manuscript.

results.result: Conditional knockout of DLK in hippocampal glutamatergic neurons does not cause discernible morphological defects. Western blot analysis confirmed significant reduction of full-length DLK protein in DLK(cKO) mice, with a truncated protein lacking essential functional domains detected at reduced levels. Histological analysis showed no differences in hippocampal morphology, CA1 pyramidal layer thickness, or microtubule patterns at P15, P60, or 1 year of age.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C42 collectively demonstrate that conditional DLK knockout does not affect hippocampal glutamatergic neuron maintenance. Western blot data (C34-C37) confirm functional knockout, while extensive immunostaining and morphological analyses (C38-C41) show no phenotypic changes across multiple timepoints. The conclusion (C42) is well-supported by converging negative results from multiple assays.

results.result: DLK overexpression causes progressive, region-specific neurodegeneration in hippocampus. DLK(iOE) mice showed approximately 3-fold increase in DLK levels and developed progressive motor deficits starting around 4 months. Histological analysis revealed dorsal CA1 pyramidal neurons were most vulnerable, showing significant thinning by P15 and near-complete loss by P60. Dentate gyrus showed delayed degeneration starting at P60, while CA3 neurons remained relatively spared even at 1 year.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C61 provide strong evidence for region-specific vulnerability to DLK overexpression. Multiple complementary approaches (RNAscope, immunostaining, NeuN staining, TUNEL) consistently demonstrate progressive CA1 degeneration beginning at P15, with quantitative measurements of pyramidal layer thickness. The dorsal-ventral gradient (C61) and relative CA3 resistance (C60) are well-documented. The temporal progression is clearly established across multiple timepoints.

results.result: DLK overexpression induces reactive gliosis in affected hippocampal regions. GFAP staining showed increased astrocyte reactivity specifically in CA1 at P15 and in CA1 and DG at P60, but not strongly in CA3. IBA1 staining revealed increased microglial reactivity around CA1, with microglia displaying more reactive morphology in DLK(iOE) compared to ramified appearance in controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 demonstrate that glial responses correlate spatially and temporally with neuronal degeneration. GFAP and IBA1 immunostaining data show region-specific increases matching the pattern of neuronal vulnerability. The morphological characterization of microglia (C64) provides additional qualitative support. These findings are consistent with expected glial responses to neurodegeneration.

results.result: RiboTag-seq analysis reveals DLK-dependent translatome in hippocampal glutamatergic neurons. 260 genes were differentially expressed in DLK(iOE) (114 up, 146 down) while only 36 genes changed in DLK(cKO) (12 up, 24 down). RRHO analysis detected significant overlap between datasets, with 17 genes showing reciprocal changes, supporting coordinated DLK-dependent regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C75 present comprehensive RiboTag-seq data with appropriate statistical thresholds (padj<0.05) and adequate sample sizes (n=3-4 per group). The asymmetry between overexpression and knockout effects is well-documented and biologically plausible. RRHO analysis (C74) provides systematic validation of coordinated regulation. The data quality metrics (>24M reads, ~14K genes detected) support reliability.

results.result: Gene ontology analysis reveals DLK regulates distinct functional gene networks. Top differentially expressed genes include Jun (transcription factor), Stmn4 (microtubule regulation), and Sh2d3c (signaling). Upregulated genes in DLK(iOE) enriched for apoptosis, cell migration, and ECM organization, while downregulated genes enriched for synaptic communication and ion transport. SynGO analysis identified 42/260 genes in DLK(iOE) involved in synaptic organization and postsynaptic signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C86 present systematic bioinformatic analysis using established tools (DAVID, SynGO). The GO enrichment patterns are internally consistent and biologically coherent, with upregulated genes relating to stress/death pathways and downregulated genes relating to synaptic function. The identification of specific gene clusters (C82-C83) and synaptic enrichment (C84-C85) is well-supported by the data. The conclusion (C86) appropriately summarizes the findings.

results.result: Spatial expression analysis reveals CA1-enriched genes are preferentially downregulated by DLK overexpression. About one-third of downregulated genes in DLK(iOE) showed CA1-enriched expression, with some (Tenm3, Lamp5, Mpped1) upregulated in DLK(cKO). GSEA analysis showed CA1 genes tended toward higher expression in DLK(cKO) versus control. However, many CA1 cell-type specification genes did not show significant downregulation with DLK overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C95 present spatial expression correlations, but the interpretation is complicated by potential confounding from neuronal death (acknowledged in C96-C97). The GSEA analysis (C92-C93) provides some support, but the lack of downregulation of cell-type specification genes (C94) and the authors' own acknowledgment of alternative interpretations (C96-C97) indicate uncertainty about whether gene downregulation is causal or consequential to degeneration. Additional experiments would be needed to establish causality.

results.result: DLK regulates c-Jun expression and phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons with regional specificity. RiboTag analysis showed Jun mRNA translation depends on DLK levels. Immunostaining revealed low basal c-Jun in control mice, with region- and age-specific patterns. In DLK(iOE) mice, c-Jun increased ~4-fold in CA1 at P15, with CA1 showing strongest response. p-c-Jun increased ~10-fold in CA1, ~6-fold in CA3, and ~8-fold in DG at P15. DLK(cKO) showed modest reductions in c-Jun and p-c-Jun, particularly in CA3.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C113 provide comprehensive evidence for DLK-dependent regulation of c-Jun through multiple complementary approaches (RiboTag-seq, immunostaining for total and phosphorylated c-Jun). The quantitative data show dose-dependent effects with regional specificity. The consistency between mRNA (C99) and protein (C100-C112) levels supports the conclusion. The modest effects in knockout (C106-C107) are appropriately acknowledged as potentially limited by detection sensitivity.

results.result: DLK specifically regulates STMN4 expression among Stathmin family members in hippocampal neurons. All four Stathmin genes were detected in the translatome, but only Stmn4 showed significant DLK-dependent regulation (upregulated in DLK(iOE), downregulated in DLK(cKO)). Western blot showed STMN4 peaks at P8 in controls. RNAscope revealed Stmn4 mRNA was strongest in CA1 pyramidal neurons and showed upregulation across all hippocampal regions in DLK(iOE) but not in DLK(cKO).
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C122 demonstrate specific regulation of STMN4 by DLK using multiple orthogonal methods (RiboTag-seq, western blot, RNAscope). The selectivity for STMN4 among family members (C115-C116) is clearly established. The spatial expression pattern (C119) and DLK-dependent changes (C120-C121) are well-documented. The speculation about masking effects in western blot (C118) is reasonable given the broad expression of STMN4.

results.result: DLK overexpression alters microtubule homeostasis in hippocampal dendrites. No changes in tyrosinated or acetylated tubulin were detected in DLK(cKO) mice. In DLK(iOE) mice, no differences were observed at P15 despite ongoing CA1 degeneration, but by P60, increased staining of both acetylated and tyrosinated tubulin was observed in apical dendrites of surviving neurons, with bright tyrosinated tubulin signals on thin branches. MAP2 staining showed similar patterns of thin branches in varied directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 document progressive microtubule alterations using multiple markers (Tuj1, tyrosinated tubulin, acetylated tubulin, MAP2). The temporal progression (no change at P15, changes at P60) is clearly established. The observation of increased both stable (acetylated) and dynamic (tyrosinated) markers (C125) is unusual but well-documented with quantification. The conclusion (C127) appropriately interprets these findings as altered homeostasis.

results.result: DLK overexpression causes mild synaptic alterations in CA1 correlating with neurodegeneration onset. In DLK(cKO), no significant differences in Bassoon/Homer1 puncta were detected. In DLK(iOE), no differences were observed at P10, but at P15, Homer1 density and size were reduced in CA1 while Bassoon remained unchanged, with overall synapse number similar. VGLUT1 analysis showed consistent patterns. CA3 showed no significant changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C138 provide systematic synapse analysis using multiple presynaptic (Bassoon, VGLUT1) and postsynaptic (Homer1) markers across multiple timepoints and regions. The quantification is rigorous with appropriate statistical analysis. The temporal correlation between synaptic changes (P15) and neurodegeneration onset is well-established. The regional specificity (CA1 affected, CA3 spared) matches the degeneration pattern. The conclusion (C137-C138) appropriately interprets the mild alterations.

results.result: DLK and STMN4 protein levels correlate in cultured hippocampal neurons. In DIV2 control neurons, DLK showed punctate localization in soma (Golgi) and neurites, particularly growth cones. STMN4 showed similar punctate patterns but appeared non-overlapping with DLK. In DLK(cKO), STMN4 patterns were similar to control. In DLK(iOE), both DLK and STMN4 levels increased with strong positive correlation (r=0.7454). STMN2 showed moderate positive correlation with DLK (r=0.4693).
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C145 demonstrate DLK-STMN4 correlation in cultured neurons using immunostaining and quantitative correlation analysis. The Spearman correlation coefficient for STMN4 (r=0.7454) indicates strong association, while STMN2 shows moderate correlation (r=0.4693). The sample sizes appear adequate (≥45-60 cells per genotype from 3 cultures). The conclusion (C145) appropriately interprets the differential correlation strengths.

results.result: DLK regulates neurite formation and axon specification in cultured hippocampal neurons. Control neurons at DIV2 typically developed multiple neurites with one axon (>90 μm). DLK(cKO) showed a trend toward more neurons without axons and significantly reduced total neurite number. DLK(iOE) showed significantly increased percentages of neurons with no axon or multiple axons, and increased numbers of thin, short neurites resembling filopodia, some showing beading suggestive of degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C153 document DLK's role in neurite formation using quantitative morphological analysis of cultured neurons. The axon specification defects are clearly demonstrated with statistical significance (C149). The neurite number changes (C148, C150) are well-quantified. The morphological descriptions (C151-C152) provide important qualitative detail. The conclusion (C153) is well-supported by the convergent findings. Sample sizes appear adequate (42-55 neurons per genotype from 3-5 cultures).

results.result: High DLK expression promotes formation of dynamic neurite branches with altered microtubule composition. Thin neurites in DLK(iOE) neurons had thin microtubule bundles without typical growth cone structures. These neurites contained tyrosinated tubulin but frequently lacked acetylated tubulin. STMN4 was present in these thin neurites, particularly in neurons with high DLK, suggesting dynamic nature.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C158 characterize the microtubule composition of aberrant neurites in DLK(iOE) neurons using multiple markers. The presence of tyrosinated tubulin (dynamic marker) and absence of acetylated tubulin (stable marker) (C155) is consistent with dynamic structures. The presence of STMN4 (C156) provides additional support. The inference about dynamic nature (C157) is reasonable based on the marker profile. The conclusion (C158) appropriately summarizes these findings.

results.result: DLK expression levels inversely correlate with dendritic spine density and maturity in cultured neurons. At DIV14, DLK(cKO) neurons showed higher spine density with significantly more mushroom spines. DLK(iOE) neurons showed reduced spine density with fewer mushroom spines and higher percentage of thin (immature) spines. Bassoon staining in DLK(iOE) was abnormal (larger, irregular), suggesting disrupted presynaptic active zones.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C165 demonstrate DLK's role in spine maturation using quantitative morphological analysis and presynaptic markers. The inverse correlation between DLK levels and spine maturity is clearly established with statistical significance. The spine classification (mushroom vs. thin) follows established criteria (referenced to Risher et al., 2014). The Bassoon abnormalities (C160-C161) provide additional evidence for synaptic disruption. Sample sizes appear adequate (30-46 neurons per genotype from 3-4 cultures).

results.result: DLK is a conserved MAP3K with versatile, context-dependent roles in neurons. DLK plays roles in neuronal development, axon injury responses, stress responses, and neurodegeneration depending on cell type and context. Emerging evidence implicates abnormal DLK signaling in neurodegenerative diseases. DLK signals through MAP2Ks (MKK4, MKK7) and MAPKs (JNK, p38, ERK) and localizes to axons, dendrites, Golgi apparatus, and transport vesicles in cultured neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C14 summarize established knowledge about DLK supported by extensive citations throughout the manuscript. These are well-established facts in the field serving as background context. The evidence type is primarily CITATION and KNOWLEDGE, which is appropriate for introductory material.

results.result: Prior studies establish diverse roles of DLK in different neuronal contexts. Constitutive DLK knockout mice die perinatally with mild developmental defects. Conditional and inducible deletions show context-specific effects on dendritic spines, synaptic strength, and responses to injury. DLK is implicated in kainic acid-induced hippocampal neuron death and Alzheimer's disease pathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C33 comprehensively review prior literature on DLK function, all supported by appropriate citations. This establishes the knowledge foundation and rationale for the current study. These are well-established findings from the literature serving as background.

results.result: DLK protein levels increase under various stress and injury conditions. Studies report DLK increases following optic nerve crush, NGF withdrawal (~2-fold), sciatic nerve injury, and ApoE4 treatment (~4-fold in induced human neurons). Increased DLK expression can lead to activation through dimerization and autophosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 summarize prior findings on DLK upregulation under stress, all supported by citations. This provides important context for the overexpression model used in the study. The activation mechanism (C47) is established knowledge. These claims appropriately set up the rationale for studying DLK overexpression effects.

results.result: DLK-induced neuronal death pattern resembles selective vulnerability in disease models. The pattern of CA1 vulnerability and CA3 resistance shares similarity with differential vulnerability reported in Alzheimer's disease patients and animal models of oxidative stress, ischemia, and glutamate excitotoxicity. The dorsal-ventral gradient also resembles ischemia models.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C170 draw appropriate comparisons between the current findings and established patterns of hippocampal vulnerability in disease models, supported by citations. These comparisons are reasonable and help contextualize the significance of the regional specificity observed. However, these are comparative/interpretive claims rather than direct experimental findings.

results.result: DLK-dependent gene expression shows cell-type specificity compared to other neuronal contexts. Loss of DLK causes modest changes in few genes while overexpression affects many genes, similar to other studies. However, hippocampal neurons show strong Jun induction without Atf3/Atf4 changes, unlike axotomized neurons. Synaptic genes (Tenm3, Nptx1, Nptxr) but not complement genes show DLK-dependence, contrasting with spinal motor neurons. Cell-type intrinsic genomic regulation may underlie these differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C179 provide thoughtful comparison of the current findings with prior transcriptomic studies in other neuronal types, appropriately supported by citations. The identification of cell-type specific differences (C174-C176) is well-documented. The speculation about genomic regulation (C177) and differential transcription factor activation (C178-C179) is reasonable interpretation, appropriately presented as speculation.

results.result: c-Jun can autoregulate its expression and may contribute to regional vulnerability differences. The c-Jun promoter has AP1 sites and c-Jun can regulate its own expression in multiple contexts (cancer cells, NGF-deprived neurons, kainic acid-treated hippocampus). DLK(iOE)-induced signal amplification may differ between CA1 and CA3, potentially explaining differential vulnerability.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C182 cite established knowledge about c-Jun autoregulation. However, C183 is speculative about mechanisms underlying regional differences. While the speculation is reasonable given the data showing stronger c-Jun induction in CA1, direct evidence for differential signal amplification is not provided. This remains a hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: DLK regulates Stathmin expression with potential roles in microtubule dynamics and neuronal morphology. Multiple studies show DLK regulates different Stathmin isoforms under injury. In hippocampus, Stmn2 is more abundant than Stmn4, with different ratios than DRG. ChIP-seq data suggest Jun binding sites in Stmn4 promoter. STMN4 expression peaks at P8, correlating with neurite outgrowth and synapse formation. DLK-dependent STMN regulation may affect cytoskeletal rearrangements, though STMN4 changes alone are unlikely to be the major factor in neuronal death.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C194 integrate current findings with prior literature on Stathmin regulation. The citations support DLK-Stathmin connections in other contexts (C184). The expression data (C185, C187) and ChIP-seq evidence (C186) are appropriately cited. The speculation about functional roles (C193) and limitations (C194) are reasonable. The acknowledgment that STMN4 alone is unlikely to explain neuronal death (C194) shows appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: DLK has conserved roles in synapse formation and maintenance across species. DLK functions in synapse formation were first revealed in C. elegans and Drosophila. The current hippocampal translatome data extends this by revealing DLK-dependent networks in synapse organization, adhesion molecules, and AMPA receptor regulation. Increased DLK alters Bassoon patterns consistent with invertebrate findings. DLK regulates dendritic spine morphology, with loss increasing mature spines and overexpression decreasing spine maturity, similar to cortical neuron studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C195-C203 effectively synthesize current findings with prior work to establish conserved DLK functions in synapse regulation. The citations to invertebrate studies (C195) and comparisons with cortical neurons (C200) are appropriate. The integration of current translatome data (C196), culture findings (C197-C199), and tissue analysis (C201) provides comprehensive support for the conclusion about conserved synaptic roles (C203).

results.result: DLK conditional knockout (DLK(cKO)) in hippocampal glutamatergic neurons results in significantly reduced full-length DLK protein, with a truncated protein lacking essential functional domains. Despite this, DLK(cKO) mice show no discernible phenotype in hippocampal morphology, neuronal positioning, microtubule organization, or behavior from birth to one year of age, indicating DLK is not essential for post-mitotic hippocampal glutamatergic neuron maintenance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accepted these findings without raising concerns. One reviewer noted the study 'demonstrates that DLK deletion had minimal effects,' and another stated the authors 'have sufficiently addressed all issues raised.' The lack of phenotype in DLK(cKO) mice is treated as a valid baseline finding.

results.result: DLK overexpression (DLK(iOE)) in hippocampal glutamatergic neurons leads to progressive, region-specific neurodegeneration. At P10, hippocampal morphology is indistinguishable from controls, but by P15, significant CA1 pyramidal layer thinning and increased TUNEL staining indicate neuronal death. By P60, most CA1 pyramidal neurons are lost, and dentate gyrus shows progressive thinning through one year. CA3 neurons appear less vulnerable throughout. DLK(iOE) mice develop progressive motor deficits starting around four months of age.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirmed this finding as a key contribution. One reviewer highlighted 'the finding that DLK may differentially impact neuronal death will become the basis for future studies exploring whether DLK contributes to differential neuronal susceptibility to death, which is a broadly important topic.' Another noted the study 'identifies: (1) CA1 vs CA3 hippocampal neurons have differing sensitivity to increased DLK signaling.' The addition of P10 data was specifically praised as 'an important advance.'

results.result: DLK(iOE) mice show increased GFAP staining (astrocyte marker) specifically in CA1 at P15 and in CA1 and DG at P60, but not as strongly in CA3. IBA1 staining (microglia marker) is increased around CA1, with microglia appearing more reactive in DLK(iOE) compared to ramified morphology in controls.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these neuroinflammatory findings, which are presented as supporting evidence for the neurodegeneration phenotype. The data are treated as confirmatory markers of the degenerative process rather than as contested findings.

results.result: RiboTag-seq analysis reveals 260 differentially expressed genes in DLK(iOE) neurons (114 up, 146 down) and 36 in DLK(cKO) neurons (12 up, 24 down). Seventeen genes overlap between conditions, with 13 upregulated in DLK(iOE) and downregulated in DLK(cKO), and 3 showing the reverse pattern. RRHO analysis detects significant overlap in genes regulated by DLK, supporting that expression of many genes is DLK-dependent.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised this work as 'a conceptual advance' in 'defining DLK-dependent changes in translation.' One reviewer stated the study 'provides interesting new insights' and specifically highlighted 'DLK-dependent signaling in these neurons is similar to but distinct from the downstream factors identified in other cell types.' The translatome findings are treated as a major strength.

results.result: The most significant differentially expressed genes in DLK(iOE) include Jun (c-Jun transcription factor), Stmn4 (Stathmin family), and Sh2d3c. Gene ontology analysis shows upregulated genes are enriched in apoptosis, cell migration, cell adhesion, and extracellular matrix organization, while downregulated genes relate to synaptic communication and ion transport. SynGO analysis reveals 42 of 260 DLK(iOE) differentially expressed genes are enriched in synaptic organization and postsynaptic receptor signaling, including AMPA receptor regulators and cell adhesion molecules.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these bioinformatic findings without challenge. One reviewer noted the study 'identified Jun and STMN4 as DLK-dependent genes that may contribute to this effect,' treating these as valid mechanistic insights. The gene ontology and pathway analyses are presented as supporting the functional interpretation of DLK's role.

results.result: About one-third of genes downregulated in DLK(iOE) show enriched expression in CA1, including Tenm3, Lamp5, and Mpped1 (which are upregulated in DLK(cKO)). Among 42 synaptic genes differentially expressed in DLK(iOE), downregulated genes show CA1 enrichment while upregulated genes are expressed across all regions. GSEA shows CA1 genes tend to be expressed more in DLK(cKO) compared to control. The authors suggest decreased expression of CA1-enriched genes may contribute to CA1 vulnerability to elevated DLK, though this could also be a secondary effect of degeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these spatial expression analyses or the interpretation of regional vulnerability. The findings are treated as supporting evidence for the differential susceptibility of CA1 vs CA3 neurons, which reviewers identified as a key contribution. The authors' acknowledgment of alternative interpretations (secondary vs. causal) is appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: c-Jun, a key downstream transcription factor in DLK/JNK signaling, shows DLK-dependent expression and phosphorylation. In DLK(iOE) mice, c-Jun immunostaining increases progressively, with the strongest increase (~fourfold) in CA1 at P15. Phosphorylated c-Jun (p-c-Jun) shows strong increases in CA1 (~tenfold), CA3 (~sixfold), and DG (~eightfold) at P15, remaining elevated at P60. In DLK(cKO), p-c-Jun levels in CA3 show significant reduction. CA1 neurons show higher dependence on DLK for Jun translation and c-Jun phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as valid mechanistic data linking DLK to downstream signaling. The c-Jun data are treated as confirmatory evidence for DLK pathway activation and are consistent with the broader translatome findings. No concerns were raised about the methodology or interpretation.

results.result: Among Stathmin family genes, only Stmn4 shows significant upregulation in DLK(iOE) and downregulation in DLK(cKO). STMN4 protein levels peak around P8 in control mice. Stmn4 mRNA is present across all hippocampal regions with strongest expression in CA1 pyramidal neurons. In DLK(iOE) mice, glutamatergic neurons in CA1, CA3, and DG show upregulation of Stmn4, while DLK(cKO) shows comparable levels to control.
results.evaluation: Reviewers specifically highlighted STMN4 as a key finding, with one noting 'the identification of STMN4 as a downstream signal' as evidence of cell-type specificity in DLK signaling. The data are treated as a significant mechanistic discovery linking DLK to cytoskeletal regulation.

results.result: Loss of DLK causes no detectable changes to microtubules (tyrosinated or acetylated tubulin) in hippocampal tissue. In DLK(iOE) mice, microtubule markers show no differences at P15 in CA1, but by P60, increased staining of both acetylated and tyrosinated tubulin is observed in apical dendrites, with bright signals on thin branches. MAP2 staining reveals thin branches extending in varied directions. The findings suggest increased DLK expression alters neuronal microtubule homeostasis and/or integrity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these microtubule findings, which are presented as supporting evidence for DLK's role in cytoskeletal regulation. The data complement the STMN4 findings and are treated as mechanistically coherent with the broader story of DLK function.

results.result: In vivo synapse analysis shows no significant differences in Bassoon and Homer1 puncta in DLK(cKO) compared to control at P60. In DLK(iOE) mice, no differences are detected at P10. At P15, Bassoon density and size in CA1 are comparable to control, but Homer1 density and size are reduced, while overall synapse number remains similar. VGLUT1 analysis shows a trend toward increased puncta in DLK(cKO) and fewer puncta in DLK(iOE). The findings suggest conditional knockout of DLK has minimal effect on glutamatergic synapses, while increased DLK leads to mild alterations in CA1 at P15, correlating with onset of neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these in vivo synapse findings without raising concerns. The data are treated as supporting evidence for the temporal progression of DLK-induced pathology, with synaptic changes preceding overt neuronal death. The P10 data addition was specifically noted as addressing reviewer concerns.

results.result: In cultured hippocampal neurons (DIV2), DLK shows punctate localization in neurites and soma (Golgi). STMN4 shows punctate pattern non-overlapping with DLK. In DLK(iOE) neurons, both DLK and STMN4 levels are increased with strong positive correlation (Spearman r=0.7454). A moderate positive correlation exists between DLK and STMN2 (r=0.4693). The data suggest DLK has a stronger effect on STMN4 levels but may also regulate STMN2.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these cultured neuron findings, which provide cellular-level validation of the in vivo translatome data. The correlation analyses are treated as supporting evidence for DLK's regulation of Stathmin family proteins.

results.result: In cultured hippocampal neurons at DIV2, DLK(cKO) shows a trend toward more neurons without axons and significantly reduced total neurite number. DLK(iOE) shows increased percentages of neurons without axons and with multiple axons, plus increased numbers of thin, short neurites resembling filopodia, some with beading appearance suggesting degeneration. These thin neurites contain tyrosinated tubulin (dynamic marker) but often lack acetylated tubulin (stable marker), and contain STMN4. The findings suggest DLK plays a role in neurite formation and axon specification, with high DLK promoting formation of short, thin, dynamic branches.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these cultured neuron morphology findings as valid. One reviewer noted the study demonstrates 'DLK overexpression resulted in morphological and synaptic abnormalities,' treating these as confirmatory evidence. The data are presented as mechanistic insights into DLK's developmental roles.

results.result: In cultured neurons at DIV14, DLK(cKO) shows no change in Bassoon puncta but increased spine density with more mushroom spines. DLK(iOE) shows abnormal Bassoon staining (larger, irregular) suggesting disrupted presynaptic active zones, reduced spine density, and more immature spines (fewer mushroom, more thin spines). Expression levels of DLK appear inversely correlated with spine density and maturity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these synapse and spine findings in culture. The data are treated as supporting evidence for DLK's role in synapse formation and maturation, complementing the in vivo findings. One reviewer noted the study demonstrates 'DLK overexpression negatively impacts synapse number.'

results.result: The pattern of DLK-induced neuronal death (CA1 vulnerability, CA3 resistance, dorsal-ventral gradient) shares similarity with differential vulnerability reported in Alzheimer's disease patients and animal models of oxidative stress, ischemia, and glutamate excitotoxicity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this comparative discussion without challenge. The similarity to disease models is treated as contextualizing the findings within broader neurodegenerative mechanisms. One reviewer noted the pattern 'will become the basis for future studies' on neuronal susceptibility.

results.result: Loss of DLK results in modest expression changes in a small number of genes, while overexpression leads to changes in a larger set. Gene ontology reveals similar terms as other DLK studies (neuron differentiation, apoptosis, ion transport, synaptic regulation), but with cell-type-specific differences: strong Jun induction but no Atf3/Atf4 changes (unlike injured neurons), no ATF4 target gene changes, synaptic genes (Tenm3, Nptx1, Nptxr) but not complement genes (unlike regenerating motor neurons). The authors suggest genomic structure and cell-type-intrinsic regulation may underlie these differences, with different transcription factor programs (JUN vs ATF3/ATF4) leading to distinct outcomes (synapse refinement vs regeneration).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed these comparative findings as demonstrating cell-type specificity. One reviewer stated the study 'identifies: (2) DLK-dependent signaling in these neurons is similar to but distinct from the downstream factors identified in other cell types, highlighted by the identification of STMN4 as a downstream signal.' The discussion of mechanistic differences is treated as appropriate scientific interpretation.

results.result: The c-Jun promoter has AP1 sites and c-Jun can regulate its own expression in various contexts (cancer cells, NGF-deprived neurons, kainic acid-treated hippocampus). The authors speculate that DLK(iOE)-induced signal transduction amplification may differ between CA1 and CA3, potentially explaining differential vulnerability.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this mechanistic speculation, which is appropriately framed as interpretation rather than definitive conclusion. The discussion of c-Jun autoregulation is supported by citations and treated as plausible mechanistic reasoning.

results.result: DLK regulates Stathmin isoforms in multiple neuron types under injury. In hippocampus, Stmn2 is expressed at higher levels than Stmn4. ChIP-seq data suggest a possible Jun binding site in the Stmn4 promoter. STMN4 expression peaks around P8, correlating with neurite outgrowth and synapse formation. The authors speculate DLK-dependent regulation of STMN4 and other STMNs may have critical roles in cytoskeletal rearrangements for neuronal morphology and synapse formation/stability, though changes in STMN4 alone are unlikely to be a major factor in regional neuron death due to Stathmin redundancy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings and interpretations without challenge. The discussion of STMN4's role is appropriately cautious, acknowledging both its significance and limitations. The data are treated as mechanistically informative while recognizing complexity.

results.result: DLK's in vivo functions were first revealed in C. elegans and Drosophila synapse formation studies. The hippocampal translatome extends this by revealing DLK-dependent networks in synapse organization, adhesion molecules, and trans-synaptic signaling (especially AMPA receptors and calcium signaling). Increased DLK alters Bassoon pattern in culture, consistent with invertebrate findings. DLK regulates dendritic spine morphology: loss of DLK increases spine density and maturity, while increased DLK reduces density and maturity. In CA1, DLK overexpression reduces Homer1 density, suggesting synaptic defects correlate with degeneration onset. The data support a conserved role for DLK in synapse formation and maintenance through regulating translation of genes involved in neuron outgrowth, synaptic adhesion, and synapse activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirmed these findings as a major contribution. One reviewer stated the study 'provides confirmatory evidence that supports previously published work through orthogonal methods, which adds additional confidence to our understanding of DLK signaling in neurons.' Another noted the findings 'will be important for scientists interested in synapse formation.' The conservation across species and the mechanistic insights are treated as significant advances.
